Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019 (Uber SubmitQueue, EuroSys 2019): with two concurrent potentially conflicting changes the model gives a 5 percent chance of a real conflict, rising to 40 percent with 16 such changes (model figures, not a count of events).
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: the iOS mainline was green only 52 percent of the time over one week before SubmitQueue, and the paper says it has 'remained green at all times' since launch.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: SubmitQueue's P50 turnaround is at most 2.98x the optimal Oracle's in the iOS replay at 100 to 500 changes per hour.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: the Speculate-all strategy reaches P50 up to 15x and P99 up to 24x the Oracle's turnaround in the same replay.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: Single-Queue at 500 changes per hour has P50, P95 and P99 turnaround 80x, 129x and 132x the Oracle's, in the same replay.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: with 500 workers at 500 changes per hour, SubmitQueue's three turnaround percentiles fall to 1.2x the Oracle's.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: the conflict analyzer improves the Oracle's turnaround by up to 60 percent, and only 20 percent for the Optimistic approach because the iOS build graph is very deep.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: SubmitQueue's throughput is up to 60 percent slower than the Oracle, about 20 percent slower with 500 workers, and Single-Queue is 95 percent slower.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: the failure model reaches 97 percent accuracy on a 30 percent hold-out.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: only 7.9 percent of changes changed the iOS monorepo build graph over five months.
Ananthanarayanan et al. 2019: 93 percent of a survey of 40 engineers believed an always-green mainline improves their personal productivity.
Juloori et al. 2025 (Uber CI at Scale, ICSE 2025) headline: CI resource usage down 53 percent, weekly CPU hours down 44 percent, and p95 waiting time down 37 percent.
note: The per-monorepo figures differ; see the next record.

claim: Juloori et al. 2025, before and after on live traffic: weekly CPU hours fall 44.70 percent (Go), 34.86 percent (iOS) and 52.23 percent (Android), and p95 wait falls 44.67, 33.32 and 31.66 percent.
Juloori et al. 2025: builds per change fall 45.45 percent (Go), 47.86 percent (iOS) and 64.02 percent (Android).
Juloori et al. 2025: an estimated 40 to 65 percent of builds are prematurely aborted across major Uber monorepos.
Juloori et al. 2025: the build-time model error (MAPE) is 3 percent for Go, 6 percent for iOS and 3.5 percent for Android.
Juloori et al. 2025: the bypass of small changes is triggered at rates from 0 to 45 percent of waiting changes.
Memon et al. 2017 (Google TAP): an average day has over 13K code projects, 800K builds and 150 million test runs, and a code commit every second on average.
Memon et al. 2017: of 5.5 million affected tests analysed over one period, only 63K ever failed.

Memon et al. 2017, Table II: 5,082,803 of 5,562,881 test targets (91.3 percent) never failed and passed at least once, and 1.23 percent of histories show a real breakage after flaky targets are removed.
Memon et al. 2017: more than 99 percent of all tests run by the CI system pass or flake.
Memon et al. 2017: less than 0.5 percent of tests fail per average change.
Memon et al. 2017: files modified within a short time span by 3 or more developers are significantly more likely to cause breakages than files modified by 2 developers.
Memon et al. 2017: one user's commits caused breakages in 59 of 182 (31.4 percent), and one release tool's in 39 of 42 commits.
Memon et al. 2017 (one-month replay): testing only targets within MinDist 10 or 6 ran 61 and 50 percent of test targets, saving 42 and 55 percent of resources, with no breakage or fix missed.
Memon et al. 2017 state it is not cost effective to test each code commit individually, which is the reason TAP batches changes.
Memon et al. 2017: per-author breakage risk differs, with 14 to 31 percent of commits by single humans causing breakages.
Winters, Manshreck and Wright 2020 (Software Engineering at Google, ch.23, summary): a change that passes presubmit has a very high likelihood (95 percent or more) of passing the rest.
Winters et al. 2020 (ch.23, summary): TAP handles over 50,000 unique changes and over 4 billion test cases a day, with an average wait to submit of about 11 minutes.
Winters et al. 2020 (ch.23, summary): running one team's end-to-end tests every two hours cut its culprit set by 12 times.
Winters et al. 2020 (ch.23, summary): a hermetic presubmit test set from Google Assistant cut runtime 14x with virtually no flakiness.
Winters et al. 2020 (ch.23, summary): mid-air collisions, two clean changes that break together, happen most days at Google's scale.

The trunkbaseddevelopment.com site (summary) says to integrate at least once per 24 hours and that Google uses trunk-based development with about 35,000 developers in one repo, and gives no figure for its effect on conflicts.
Zuul speculative gating (OpenStack project docs, summary): each project queue starts with a window of 20 changes, grows by 1 per merge and halves per failure; the page gives no throughput numbers.
GitHub merge queue (GitHub docs, summary): merge limit and build concurrency each range from 1 to 100, and the page gives no performance numbers.
Najafi, Shang and Rigby 2019 (FSE, Ericsson, summary): constant batch sizes cut execution or resource use by 42 percent or 47 percent, and which of the two figures is right was not confirmed.

Concordia 2023 (parallel batch testing, Ericsson data and 276 million Chrome test outcomes, summary): a constant batch of 4 needs up to 72 percent fewer machines at the same average feedback time, dynamic batching up to 91 percent fewer, and test-case batching up to 81 percent fewer.
FONTE (culprit ranking, summary): ranks the real bug-inducing commit in the top five for 87 percent of studied batch failures.
Machalica et al. 2019 (Facebook PTS): almost 99.9 percent of test targets selected by build-dependency-based selection pass.
Machalica et al. 2019 (Facebook PTS): predictive selection selects fewer than a third of the tests that build dependencies would select.

Machalica et al. 2019 (Facebook PTS): predictive test selection catches over 95 percent of individual test failures and over 99.9 percent of faulty code changes, where faulty means any selected test fails.
Machalica et al. 2019 (Facebook PTS): predictive selection reduces the total infrastructure cost of change-based testing by a factor of two.
Machalica et al. 2019 (Facebook PTS): training uses outcomes of changes from the past three months, and the calibration is TestRecall above 0.95 and ChangeRecall above 0.999 at land time.
Machalica et al. 2019 (Facebook PTS): training on flaky test results gives very poor predictions.

Elbaum et al. 2014: pre-submit selection with failure window Wf of 96 detects 70 to 80 percent of failing test suites, leaving 20 to 30 percent unselected, on a replay of over 3.5 million suite executions over 30 days.
Elbaum et al. 2014: random selection of the same number of test suites performed about six times worse in failure detection.
Elbaum et al. 2014: at a 0.5 percent suite failure rate, selecting 33 percent of suites moves a post-submit load of less than 0.17 percent of the pre-submit testing load.
Elbaum et al. 2014: high-priority requests range from 5 to 8 percent.
note: The file does not say what the 5 to 8 percent is a share of.

claim: Gligoric et al. 2015 (Ekstazi): over 615 revisions of 32 open-source projects (almost 5 million LOC), end-to-end testing time falls 32 percent on average and 54 percent for longer-running suites, against running all tests.
Gligoric et al. 2015 (Ekstazi): with the collection phase run off-line, the reduction is 47 percent on average and 66 percent for longer-running suites.

Gligoric et al. 2015 (Ekstazi): the time for the AEC variant varies between 9 and 138 percent (slowdown), all slowdowns are for short-running suites, and the average is 68 percent of RetestAll (46 percent for long suites).
Gligoric et al. 2015 (Ekstazi): on Cucumber, Ekstazi selects 12 percent of test entities but its time is 99 percent of RetestAll.
Memon et al. 2017 (TAP): of 115,160 test targets that both passed and failed at least once, 46,694 are flakes.

Micco 2016 (Google Testing Blog, summary): about 1.5 percent of all test runs report a flaky result, and almost 16 percent of 4.2 million tests have some flakiness, as cited by academic papers; the blog page itself returned only comments.
Luo et al. FSE 2014 (writer's recall, to be checked): of 201 flaky-test fixes, the leading causes are async wait, concurrency and test order, at about 45, 20 and 12 percent.
Brun et al. 2013 (Crystal, TSE): one in six merges, 16 percent, had textual conflicts and the other 83 percent had none, across nine open-source systems totaling 3.4 million lines.

Brun et al. 2013 (Crystal, TSE): over 5,355 merges in Git, Perl5 and Voldemort, 76 percent completed cleanly, 16 percent had a textual conflict, 1 percent a build failure and 6 percent a test failure.
Brun et al. 2013 (Crystal, TSE): 266 textual conflicts are 67 percent of all conflicts, and the paper says '33 percent of the 399 clean textual merges led to build or test conflicts'.
Brun et al. 2013 (Crystal, TSE): conflicts persist on average 3.2 days (the paper's contributions list says 3 days).
Brun et al. 2013 (Crystal, TSE): for 19 percent of the commits an earlier merge would have conflicted.

Kasi et al. 2013 (Cassandra, ICSE): across four projects of 88 to 505 merges each, merge conflicts range from 7.6 to 19.3 percent, 2.1 to 14.7 percent of clean merges had build failures, and 5.6 to 35 percent of correct builds had test failures.
Kasi et al. 2013 (Cassandra), Table I: Perl had 14 of 185 merges with conflicts and 56 test failures (30.2 percent), and Voldemort had 55 of 380 (14.5 percent) with 133 test failures (35 percent).
Kasi et al. 2013 (Cassandra): the task scheduler avoided a majority of conflicts in simulations on past data, for example 16/17 to 33/35 avoided in one table.
Shen, Gulzar et al. 2023 (TOSEM, summary): across 208 repositories, 15,886 scenarios had textual conflicts, 79 had build conflicts and 33 had test conflicts, with the denominator unclear.
Lessenich et al. 2017 (ASE, summary): across 155 projects and 32,579 merge scenarios, none of seven developer-suggested indicators predicts conflict frequency.
Dias et al. 2019 (summary): 267,657 merge scenarios from 744 repositories, where conflicts are rare, so prediction faces class imbalance.
Vale, Costa and Apel 2023 (summary, one study): across 66 projects, combined technical and social features reached accuracy 0.92 and recall 1.00 for conflict prediction.
Cataldo and Herbsleb 2013 (IEEE TSE, summary only): coordination gaps significantly increased software failures in two projects at two companies; the effect size was not obtained.
Mauerer et al. 2021 (arXiv 2105.08198): across 25 large open-source projects, socio-technical misalignment is not related to project bugs or churn in any temporal scenario.
Mauerer et al. 2021: no statistical relationship between the alignment of developer tasks and communications and project outcomes.
Bird et al. 2011 (Windows Vista and Windows 7): a minor contributor is a developer whose share of commits to a component is below 5 percent.

Bird et al. 2011: Spearman correlation with failures is 0.86, 0.70, 0.93 and 0.25 for minor contributors and 0.84, 0.70, 0.92 and 0.24 for total developers (Vista pre, Vista post, Win7 pre, Win7 post).
Bird et al. 2011: the top owner's share correlates -0.49, -0.49, -0.29 and -0.02 with failures (Vista pre, Vista post, Win7 pre, Win7 post), the last not significant.

Bird et al. 2011: code metrics alone explain 26, 29, 24 and 18 percent of variance in failures; adding minor contributors raises this to 46, 41, 70 and 21 percent, and the final models reach up to 72 percent.

Kasi et al. 2013 (Cassandra): resolving the merge conflicts took substantial effort, typically spanning multiple days.
